Beyond charity: The UAE initiative rewriting the rules of giving | The National

For Maywand Jabarkhyl, chief executive of FBMI, the future of philanthropy is not about asking for donations, but creating products people genuinely want to buy

Actual Article Body:
For Maywand Jabarkhyl, chief executive of FBMI, the future of philanthropy is not about asking for donations, but creating products people genuinely want to buy

For Maywand Jabarkhyl, chief executive of FBMI, the future of philanthropy is not about asking for donations, but creating products people genuinely want to buy

October 26, 2026

For more than 15 years, the Fatima bint Mohamed Bin Zayed Initiative (FBMI) has been rethinking philanthropy. Founded in 2010 by Sheikha Fatima bint Mohamed, it asks a fundamental question: rather than simply giving money to communities in need, what if aid could create livelihoods that eventually sustain themselves?

Its model is deceptively simple: create products people want to buy, connect their makers with international markets, and reinvest the profits in healthcare, education and support for disadvantaged communities.

“We have to change the way the world gives money,” says Maywand Jabarkhyl, chief executive of FBMI.

“You can look at profit in a very positive manner. You just have to make sure that it’s ethical and responsible.”

Rather than beginning with a community and asking what can be donated, FBMI first looks for gaps in the retail market.

“When you look at the philanthropic environment anywhere in the world, the focus is strictly on fundraising,” says Jabarkhyl.

“What we have done is look at the market first and found a solution based on consumer demands. We give the women in our programmes access to international global markets, so that their products can be upscaled, and they can earn a good living.”

FBMI’s model is closer to a social enterprise. Women in disadvantaged communities are trained to produce goods to international standards; the products are then sold through a commercial network, with profits reinvested in the wider programme.

FBMI works with carpet weavers and rural farms, and has a client roster that includes five-star hotels, luxury brands and Emirates airline. Produce from rural Afghanistan and Tanzania is now served in the Emirates first class cabin.

“I don’t think it can become much bigger than this,” says Jabarkhyl.

The UAE’s leadership has also embraced the initiative, commissioning carpets as gifts for international dignitaries including former US president Joe Biden, former French president Nicolas Sarkozy and the late Pope Francis. The pontiff received the Tolerance Carpet, handwoven by Afghan women, from President Sheikh Mohamed.

“We’ve become a tool for diplomacy,” says Jabarkhyl. Soft power, it seems, has been made tangible. But FBMI’s ambitions extend beyond carpets. Since launching its strategic advisory arm in 2015, it has developed four areas of activity: healthcare, education, arts and culture, and strategic advisory – alongside a portfolio of social enterprises.

Its healthcare work reaches more than 25,000 people each month through services including mother-and-child clinics and vaccination programmes focused on 11 diseases, including polio. Other projects have improved sanitation and access to water, supported Tanzanian farmers and provided digital education for Afghan girls unable to attend school.

FBMI has hosted talks at the World Economic Forum’s Annual Meeting in Davos, worked with UN agencies including Unicef and UNHCR, and collaborated on limited-edition carpets with Zaha Hadid and Norma Kamali, as well as regional and Emirati creatives including Roudha Al Shamsi and Nada Debs.

It is now seeking to establish handmade carpet weaving within the UAE’s contemporary cultural landscape. In Abu Dhabi, FBMI is developing a centre dedicated to arts, crafts, heritage and design, exploring how traditional Emirati materials and techniques can be adapted for a contemporary market.

Another initiative, Intimaa: Sacred Threads, coincides with the Year of the Family. Ten UAE residents and artists, including Shamsa Al Omaira, Dhabia Al Qubaisi, Azza Al Sherif and Noura Al Serkal, are designing carpets to be woven by women in Afghanistan. The finished works will be exhibited at the Cultural Foundation in Abu Dhabi before being auctioned in December.

Another project will explore the intersection of Emirati weaving traditions such as Talli and Al-Sadu – both part of Unesco’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list – with hand-knotted carpets. FBMI also hopes to revive traditional methods of processing goat and camel wool in the region.

The work at the intersection of craft and art is also being recognised beyond the traditional non-profit space. “We’re going to be at Frieze Abu Dhabi in November, which is huge, of course,” Jabarkhyl says.

This breadth reflects the organisation’s evolution. What began as a carpet-weaving project in 2010 has become a broader experiment in how commerce, culture and philanthropy can coexist. FBMI plans to expand its commercial model to another 50 regions, with research already under way in Kenya, Senegal and Kurdistan.

The organisation’s market-first philosophy may be FBMI’s most radical proposition. Instead of asking consumers to buy something because it is charitable, it asks them to buy a product because it is good – and then allows the social impact to follow.

“You don’t have to just focus on corporate profits and then give the chunk away to a charity,” Jabarkhyl says. “You can do it all.” The proposition appears to be working. FBMI is on track to generate a nine-figure revenue this year, helping to fund its healthcare, education, research and development programmes.

Jabarkhyl’s goal is not simply for FBMI to grow, but for its approach to become commonplace. “I’d like to see more organisations undertaking the model that we have,” he says. “We just can’t keep asking for more and more money every year when it comes to livelihoods.

“We are very good at saying: ‘We don’t want your money; just buy the products that we have, because they are world-class.’ I think people warm to that.

“We want to give them something in return – a lovely carpet, some nice dried fruits or saffron. When people see that there’s an exchange, they are more convinced they are doing something for the country, for arts and culture, and supporting something that they believe in.”

That is the philosophy at the heart of FBMI. Its proposition is not that philanthropy should disappear, but that it should become more ambitious: less concerned with the temporary relief of giving and more interested in building something that lasts.

Trick-or-treating, like most expenses recently, will come with a bigger price tag this Halloween.

Candy prices rose 7.7% over the year through September, more than twice the overall inflation rate of 3.7%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The figure tracks candy and chewing gum broadly, rather than Halloween-specific products.

But higher prices haven’t pushed candy out of the Halloween budget.

The National Retail Federation expects Americans to spend $4.1 billion on candy this year as part of a record $13.5 billion in overall Halloween spending. Its survey found that 96% of Halloween shoppers plan to buy sweets.

Americans are expected to spend $4.1 billion on Halloween candy this year, even as prices rise faster than overall inflation. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The NRF found that 31% of shoppers plan to comparison shop if prices are higher than expected, while 26% will look for coupons or sales. Retailers are offering products across a range of price points to help shoppers celebrate within their budgets, Zeller said.

NIQ said rising costs for housing, transportation and everyday essentials are shaping spending decisions, but Halloween remains an occasion consumers are willing to protect.

That resilience showed up in last year’s sales. Halloween confectionery sales rose 7.6% in 2025 even as unit sales fell 2.5%, suggesting shoppers spent more while taking home fewer items. Chocolate had the largest average unit-price increase among the confectionery categories NIQ tracked, at 11.5%.

The National Retail Federation found that 31% of shoppers plan to compare prices if Halloween candy costs more than expected. (Sarah L. Voisin/The Washington Post/Getty Images)

"Consumers continue to make room for Halloween. What’s changing is how they participate," said Chris Costagli, NIQ’s vice president of food and beverage thought leadership. Shoppers are starting earlier, spreading purchases across more trips and evaluating items more carefully, he said.

Exclusive: National Crime Victimization Survey Shows Violent Crime Plummeted in 2025

Serious violent and property crime rates took a sharp dive in 2025, dropping 25 percent and 19 percent, respectively, according to preliminary Justice Department findings obtained exclusively by Breitbart News.
The post Exclusive: National Crime Victimization Survey Shows Violent Crime Plummeted in 2025 appeared first on Breitbart.

Actual Article Body:
Serious violent and property crime rates took a sharp dive in 2025, dropping 25 percent and 19 percent, respectively, according to preliminary Justice Department findings obtained exclusively by Breitbart News.

The estimates show roughly 669,000 fewer victimizations involving rape or sexual assault, robbery, and aggravated assault than in 2024. Households also experienced about 3.5 million fewer property crimes over the same 12-month span.

The Bureau of Justice Statistics report puts the rate of violent victimization excluding simple assault at 7.4 per 1,000 residents age 12 and older, down from 9.9 in 2024. The estimated number of those victimizations declined from about 2.83 million to 2.16 million.

Robbery victimizations dropped from 626,420 down to 453,870, marking about 172,000 fewer incidents as the robbery rate fell from 2.2 to 1.6 per 1,000 residents.

Across the broader violent crime category, which includes simple assault, total victimizations fell from 8.2 million down to roughly 7.5 million in 2025. That pushed the overall rate from 28.7 to 25.7 per 1,000 people, though researchers flagged the change as statistically non-significant. Simple assaults accounted for most of those offenses, totaling 5.33 million cases.

Property crimes dropped across all major categories. Households experienced 14.89 million property victimizations, down from 18.37 million in 2024, pushing the rate down from 138 to 111.2 per 1,000 households.

Burglary and trespassing fell by about 460,000 cases to 1.41 million, dropping the rate 25 percent to 10.5 per 1,000 households. Vehicle thefts slid from 1.19 million to 841,130 — a 349,000-car reduction that put the vehicle-theft rate down roughly 30 percent. General household theft also fell 19 percent, dropping from 13.93 million to 11.41 million cases.

The Census Bureau conducts the survey annually for BJS, interviewing victims directly to capture crimes missing from police records. It excludes homicides because it relies on victim interviews, but covers attempted, threatened, and completed offenses.

The survey findings track alongside separate FBI data showing drops in crimes recorded by law enforcement, though the survey recorded much larger declines. For instance, police-reported aggravated assaults dropped 7.2 percent in FBI figures, compared to the survey’s 31 percent drop.

The source notes indicate that this divergence shows the true crime rate is falling faster than reported numbers suggest, attributing the shift to higher police solve rates that encourage victims to report crimes more frequently. The DOJ report notes that because the two collection systems measure crime differently, the gap between their numbers does not by itself establish changes in victim reporting habits.

The declines occurred during President Donald Trump’s first year back in office as federal authorities expanded border enforcement and targeted violent offenders, drug rings, and illegal firearms.

The White House reported a border surge in January 2026, announcing that over 400,000 illegal immigrants charged with or convicted of crimes were deported during Trump’s first year back in office. Administration officials credited the enforcement push and a steep drop in illegal crossings for shifting national public safety, adding that heightened enforcement created a deterrent effect against crime among undocumented immigrants remaining in the country.

Federal agencies also logged significant upticks in enforcement operations. Testifying before the Senate Judiciary Committee in September 2025, FBI Director Kash Patel stated agents seized over 1,600 kilograms of fentanyl — a 25 percent jump over 2024 — while disrupting approximately 1,800 gangs and criminal enterprises.

Patel linked the falling crime numbers to pulling agents out of headquarters to flood high-density areas. Additionally, the ATF reported a 57 percent surge in federal criminal charges under six firearms-trafficking statutes in 2025, attributing the increase to focused enforcement on repeat violent offenders, criminal organizations, and illegal gun networks.

The findings remain preliminary, with final 2025 estimates expected in 2027. BJS fully adopted a redesigned survey in January 2025 and used comparable redesigned-survey estimates for its 2024 comparison. The bureau said that the new estimates cannot be compared directly with the older survey series, limiting claims that the declines were the largest since 1973.

Serious violent and property crime rates took a sharp dive in 2025, dropping 25 percent and 19 percent, respectively, according to preliminary Justice Department findings obtained exclusively by Breitbart News.

The estimates show roughly 669,000 fewer victimizations involving rape or sexual assault, robbery, and aggravated assault than in 2024. Households also experienced about 3.5 million fewer property crimes over the same 12-month span.

The Bureau of Justice Statistics report puts the rate of violent victimization excluding simple assault at 7.4 per 1,000 residents age 12 and older, down from 9.9 in 2024. The estimated number of those victimizations declined from about 2.83 million to 2.16 million.

Robbery victimizations dropped from 626,420 down to 453,870, marking about 172,000 fewer incidents as the robbery rate fell from 2.2 to 1.6 per 1,000 residents.

Across the broader violent crime category, which includes simple assault, total victimizations fell from 8.2 million down to roughly 7.5 million in 2025. That pushed the overall rate from 28.7 to 25.7 per 1,000 people, though researchers flagged the change as statistically non-significant. Simple assaults accounted for most of those offenses, totaling 5.33 million cases.

Property crimes dropped across all major categories. Households experienced 14.89 million property victimizations, down from 18.37 million in 2024, pushing the rate down from 138 to 111.2 per 1,000 households.

Burglary and trespassing fell by about 460,000 cases to 1.41 million, dropping the rate 25 percent to 10.5 per 1,000 households. Vehicle thefts slid from 1.19 million to 841,130 — a 349,000-car reduction that put the vehicle-theft rate down roughly 30 percent. General household theft also fell 19 percent, dropping from 13.93 million to 11.41 million cases.

The Census Bureau conducts the survey annually for BJS, interviewing victims directly to capture crimes missing from police records. It excludes homicides because it relies on victim interviews, but covers attempted, threatened, and completed offenses.

The survey findings track alongside separate FBI data showing drops in crimes recorded by law enforcement, though the survey recorded much larger declines. For instance, police-reported aggravated assaults dropped 7.2 percent in FBI figures, compared to the survey’s 31 percent drop.

The source notes indicate that this divergence shows the true crime rate is falling faster than reported numbers suggest, attributing the shift to higher police solve rates that encourage victims to report crimes more frequently. The DOJ report notes that because the two collection systems measure crime differently, the gap between their numbers does not by itself establish changes in victim reporting habits.

The declines occurred during President Donald Trump’s first year back in office as federal authorities expanded border enforcement and targeted violent offenders, drug rings, and illegal firearms.

The White House reported a border surge in January 2026, announcing that over 400,000 illegal immigrants charged with or convicted of crimes were deported during Trump’s first year back in office. Administration officials credited the enforcement push and a steep drop in illegal crossings for shifting national public safety, adding that heightened enforcement created a deterrent effect against crime among undocumented immigrants remaining in the country.

Federal agencies also logged significant upticks in enforcement operations. Testifying before the Senate Judiciary Committee in September 2025, FBI Director Kash Patel stated agents seized over 1,600 kilograms of fentanyl — a 25 percent jump over 2024 — while disrupting approximately 1,800 gangs and criminal enterprises.

Patel linked the falling crime numbers to pulling agents out of headquarters to flood high-density areas. Additionally, the ATF reported a 57 percent surge in federal criminal charges under six firearms-trafficking statutes in 2025, attributing the increase to focused enforcement on repeat violent offenders, criminal organizations, and illegal gun networks.

The findings remain preliminary, with final 2025 estimates expected in 2027. BJS fully adopted a redesigned survey in January 2025 and used comparable redesigned-survey estimates for its 2024 comparison. The bureau said that the new estimates cannot be compared directly with the older survey series, limiting claims that the declines were the largest since 1973.
